About this report 
Statement of compliance 
This Climate-related Disclosure Statement (this Statement) is made by The Hollard Insurance 
Company Pty Ltd New Zealand Branch (NZBN 942 904 212 9851, NZ Company No. 5869665) (HNZ), 
under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 (the Act) for the financial year ended 30 June 2025 
(Reporting Period). This statement complies with Aotearoa New Zealand Climate Standards (NZ CS 
1, 2 and 3) issued by the External Reporting Board (XRB).  
HNZ operates as a New Zealand branch of the Australian company The Hollard Insurance Company 
Pty Ltd (ABN 78 090 584 473) (HIC), a licensed insurer under the Insurance (Prudential Supervision) 
Act 2010.  Hollard Holdings Australia Pty Ltd. (ABN 30 154 586 802) (HHA or Hollard) is HIC’s 
immediate parent company.  
For the purposes of this report, Hollard Holdings Australia Pty Ltd (Hollard, HHA, we, us or our) 
encompasses both the Australian and New Zealand businesses, and HNZ refers exclusively the New 
Zealand branch, which is in scope for this report. 
Adoption provisions 
This climate-related disclosure is prepared with reliance on the original Adoption Provisions in NZ 
CS 2 and the amended NZ CS 2 issued on November 2024 as tabled below: 
Adoption Provision 
Adoption provision 2: This exempts HNZ from disclosing anticipated climate related financial impacts 
Adoption provision 4: This exempts HNZ from disclosing its Scope 3 GHG emissions (all 15 categories) 
Adoption provision 5: This adoption provision further exempts the disclosure of comparatives for Scope 3 
GHG emissions  
Adoption provision 6: This adoption provision permits an entity to provide one year of comparative 
information for each metric 
Adoption provision 7: This exempts HNZ from disclosing an analysis of trends 
Adoption provision 8: This permits exclusion of Scope 3 GHG emission from the scope of assurance 
engagement (New for FY25) 
Disclaimer  
This report contains forward looking statements including climate scenario analysis, estimations and 
forecasts of physical and transition risks across multiple time horizons based on climate hazard 
projections for HNZ using a range of projections from multiple models.  
HNZ acknowledges that climate projections are based on assumptions about future greenhouse gas 
emissions associated with human activity and other policy choices. The climate projections do not 
attempt to predict the timing of meteorological events such as storms, droughts, or floods.

Strategy 
As a general insurer, HNZ underwrites a broad range of insurance products including motor, home, 
contents, business, bicycle and pet insurance, which are distributed through our partners including 
Ando, PetSure, Velosure and Allianz Partners.  Under Hollard’s partnership distribution model, these 
partners are delegated authority to undertake various activities on behalf of HNZ, such as marketing, 
pricing, sales, claims management, and servicing customers. 
Climate-related risks & opportunities 
Climate-related physical risks 
Climate-related physical risks relate to an increasing frequency and severity of physical hazards.  
They can be acute, such as extreme rain and floods, cyclones, storms, storm surges, and bushfires, 
or chronic, such as sea level rise.  
The acute and chronic physical climate-related risks to which HNZ’s is exposed include: 
• Acute physical risks: extreme rain and flood, bushfires, storms, and cyclones; 
• Chronic physical risks: rising sea-level and increases in temperature.  
HNZ is exposed to physical risks via the assets that it insures.  Our customers are exposed to physical 
climate risks through damage to, and loss of, insured assets such as motor vehicles and homes. The 
increasing frequency and severity of weather events over time may outstrip Hollard’s ability to 
provide affordable insurance products or deliver the expected levels of customer service. This has 
the potential to exacerbate customer vulnerability, undermine Hollard’s reputation and could 
potentially result in portfolio attrition due to customer defection, and therefore a loss of market 
share.  The potential impacts of climate risk are outlined in the diagram below.  
 
HNZ does not own any property, plant and equipment or right-of-use leased assets, therefore no 
physical assets are directly exposed to climate-related physical risks. 
Climate-related transition risks 
Transition risks are those associated with the transition to a lower-carbon economy, and can be 
categorized as: 
• Market 
• Policy and Legal  
• Technology 
• Reputation 
Hollard maintains qualitative analysis of transition risks due to the uncertainties and limitations in 
quantifying macroeconomic trends. Our highest-rated, Market risk, is associated with Hollard’s risk 
of losing market share due to a failure to keep up with changing consumer preferences for insurance 
products that either incentivise decarbonisation or support climate resilience.   
Technology risk associated with poor data quality could negatively impact the accuracy of our 
catastrophe modelling, leading to materially incorrect re/insurance pricing and placements and 
therefore increase our exposure to climate-related risk (relative to what we believe our exposure 
to be).

Climate-related opportunities 
HNZ has not identified any climate-related opportunities that it expects to materialise in the short 
term. We anticipate opportunities to innovate our products in response to changing market and 
consumer sentiment over a medium to long-term horizon.  
Climate-related strategy 
HNZ shares an overarching strategy with the broader Hollard consolidated group. Hollard continues 
to focus on developing technological capabilities and capacity for scale and efficiency to build 
impactful insurance innovation for our Australian and New Zealand customers, partners, and 
communities.  
Externally, the impact of increasing frequency of natural perils, continued claims inflation and 
heightened regulatory focus will remain challenging for Hollard and the wider insurance industry.  
Hollard has focused on aligning its sustainability initiatives with the Insurance Council of New 
Zealand (ICNZ) and the Insurance Council of Australia (ICA) to ensure we contribute to industry 
collaboration on climate change issues in a consistent approach. In FY25, Hollard joined the Hazard 
Insurance Partnership (HIP), a collaborative initiative between the Australian Government and the 
insurance industry, managed by National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), to identify 
mitigation and resilience opportunities to reduce risks in natural and built environment. 
In recent years, insurance affordability has become a pressing issue in both Australia and New 
Zealand, disproportionately impacting vulnerable communities. Through the HIP, Hollard 
contributed to the data asset being developed by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) to further 
understand the drivers of insurance affordability, availability, and coverage to support policy 
development about risk reduction and other interventions to address these issues.  
Internally, Hollard is continuously challenging our costs of doing business (e.g. investing in digital 
capabilities) to alleviate pricing pressures for customers; challenging the notion of home insurance 
product design (e.g. coverage and excesses) to remove upwards pricing pressure wherever possible; 
working towards incorporating risk mitigation discounts at a household level; and ensuring effects 
of climate change are considered in all business, investment and underwriting decisions by 
embedment into key policies and frameworks.  We have embedded climate considerations and the 
concept of responsible investments into our investment management policies and frameworks.  
In our FY24 Climate disclosure, we referenced our Shared Value Strategy and Roadmap.  Shared 
Value was, and remains, a way to think about how Hollard does well by doing good; how we become 
a catalyst for enduring, positive, social change while running a sustainable and profitable business.  
Whilst Shared Value incorporates climate related considerations, it covers a much broader range of 
sustainability topics than climate.  During FY25, key elements of Hollard’s Shared Value Strategy and 
Roadmap were operationalized via embedment into business-as-usual activities.  The focus during 
FY25 was on activities that drive action towards greater accessibility and affordability of our 
products, as noted above.  Other FY25 Shared Value activities are outside the scope of this report.

Climate scenario analysis 
In FY25, Hollard reassessed the climate scenarios developed in FY241 and reaffirmed their relevancy 
and applicability for this reporting period.  This included the review of the climate scenario analysis 
by the Board Risk Committee (BRC) and approval by the Board, with the review and approval being 
incorporated into the review or approval of the overall climate disclosure.  
HNZ continued to select 2030, 2040 and 2050 as the time horizons2 for climate scenario analysis, 
based on the tenure of HNZ’s existing partnerships, its strategic planning timeframe and assessing 
meaningful timeframes where there has been material development in the climate scenarios to 
compare across the scenarios.  
The standalone climate scenario analysis has not been formally integrated within the Group’s 
strategy. However, the impact of catastrophe risk on capital is assessed as part of Group’s regular 
scenario analysis and stress testing in line with the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process 
(ICAAP).

When determining the global warming scenarios, HNZ considered: 
• Industry specificity: ensuring our climate scenario analysis is aligned to industry bodies and to 
be easily compared with peers. This led to the adoption of the Orderly (NGFS Net-Zero 2050), 
Disorderly (NGFS Delayed Transition) and Hot House World (NGFS Current Policies) scenarios.  
• The requirements of NZ CS 1: NZ CS 1 requires the adoption of a minimum of three warming 
scenarios, including a 1.5 degrees Celsius climate-related scenario, a three degrees Celsius or 
greater climate-related scenario, and a third climate-related scenario.  
• Inclusion of a balanced spread of the scenarios: low warming ([SSP1- RCP 1.9]), medium 
warming ( [SSP2 – RCP 4.5]), and high warming ([SSP3 – RCP 7.0]) scenarios.  
Transition plan 
Based on NZ CS 1, transition plan is “an aspect of an entity’s overall strategy that describes an 
entity’s targets, including any interim targets, and actions for its transition towards a low-emissions, 
climate resilient future.”  
HNZ has zero tCO2-e of scope 1 and scope 2 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions3.  As such, we have 
no climate targets (see details in Metrics & Targets).  HNZ’s transition plan will be developed as part 
of the transition plan developed for the broader HHA entity.

Measuring risks and opportunities 
Hollard considers climate-related physical and transition risks to be material for our New Zealand 
operations in the short, medium and long term.  
HNZ currently does not underwrite any energy generation or mining related activities, does not own 
any physical assets, does not incur capital expenditure nor allocate funding directly towards 
climate-related risks. 
For the year ended 30 June 2025, HNZ has 0 tCO2-e Scope 1 and Scope 2 GHG emissions.  As such, 
we have not set climate targets, or intensity metrics. We have also applied Adoption Provision 4 
from NZ CS 2 to delay Scope 3 emissions disclosure to FY26.

Measurement approach 
HNZ has applied the Greenhouse Gas Protocol: A Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard 
(Revised Edition) (the ‘GHG Protocol’) as the measurement standard for the year ended 30 June 
2025 to measure its Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions and has adopted the financial control 
consolidation approach for assessing its GHG emissions boundary in FY25.  This differs from FY24 
when the operational control approach was adopted.  Whilst the change in consolidation approach 
could theoretically alter our emissions boundary, the outcomes of both methodologies result in the 
same overall emissions boundary being defined.  This change is in preparation for mandatory 
climate reporting in Australia to ensure consistency within the Hollard group. 
HNZ has no owned or controlled physical assets in New Zealand, and we have no leased office in 
FY25. No part of HNZ’s value chain has been excluded for assessing Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions. 
We initiated the work on scope 3 calculation in FY24 and completed scope 3 relevancy and 
materiality assessment in early FY25. It was determined that claims supply chain emissions, financed 
emissions and insurance-associated emissions are the most material categories for HNZ, and we 
have commenced engagement with business partners to better understand data availability to 
refine our workplan for FY26 reporting.  
We currently do not have an internal emission price. HNZ is applying NZ CS 2 Adoption Provision 5 
and 7 to be exempted from disclosing comparative information and trends for Scope 3 GHG 
emissions.   
Linkage of climate metrics and targets to remuneration 
KPIs in relation to monitoring, assessing and managing climate-related risks and opportunities are 
not explicitly linked to management remuneration for FY25. However, management’s remuneration 
is linked to the financial performance of the Hollard group, and that financial performance is directly 
influenced by physical climate-related risk.

Governance 
The Hollard Board oversees climate-related risks and opportunities in accordance with our 
governance framework. The Hollard Board has delegated certain responsibilities in relation to 
climate risk oversight to Board Committees as set out in the Hollard Climate Governance Oversight 
and Responsibilities diagram below. See Figure 1. Climate Governance Oversight and 
Responsibilities and Figure 2. HNZ’s Climate Risk Management for details.

During FY25, the BRC received updates through standing quarterly meetings, in relation to climate-
related impacts, climate risk management and climate-related disclosures. The Board Audit 
Committee (BAC) has received updates in relation to the external assurance outcome of scope 1 
and 2 greenhouse gas emissions.  
The ELT is accountable for executing the overall strategy, setting clear objectives and monitoring 
progress. The ELT meets monthly to monitor, escalate, and manage current and emerging risks,

The Board undertakes an annual Board Skills Assessment, which includes an assessment of 
Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) skills across our Board members to provide an overall 
view of expertise.  
The Board continues to engage with subject matter experts internally and externally to address any 
gaps in climate capabilities, and to ensure appropriate skills and competencies are in place to 
provide oversight of climate-related risks and opportunities.

Risk Management   
Risk Management Framework 
Hollard maintains a Risk Management Framework (RMF) that provides a structure for identifying, 
assessing, and managing material risks.  This ensures Hollard’s risks are being prudently and 
appropriately managed, having regard to the size, business mix and complexity of its operations. 
Hollard’s RMF applies to all entities within Hollard (including HNZ) and includes the consideration 
of risk management within its value chain.  
Hollard’s Risk Management Strategy (RMS) and Risk Appetite Statement (RAS) are key components 
of the RMF. The RMS describes each material risk (both financial and non-financial) and outlines 
Hollard’s approach to managing these risks. The RAS sets out the degree of risk Hollard is prepared 
to accept in pursuit of its strategic objectives and business plans and sets out an appetite for each 
of the material risks referenced in the RMS. Climate risk management is an integral part of Hollard’s 
everyday operations as a general insurer. Hollard's RMS and RAS include climate in the descriptions 
of our risk categories.  
During FY25, Hollard tracked climate-related risk management activities in relation to our business-
as-usual (BAU) operation in the Climate Risk Management Processes & Activities Register.  The fact 
that climate is embedded into a range of BAU activities demonstrates an integrated approach in 
identifying, assessing and managing climate risks according to established RMS risk categories (e.g. 
Underwriting, Pricing, Catastrophe, Claims, Capital and Strategic Risks).  
Hollard’s risk management approach focuses on the shorter time horizon (less than 1 year) in 
managing its material risks and will consider a longer-term horizon (more than 1 year) in managing 
its emerging material risks (including the compounding effect of physical and transition risk) in the 
long term. 
Climate risk management governance 
The Hollard Board is ultimately responsible for Hollard's RMF and oversees its operation by 
management. In particular, the Hollard Board is responsible for setting Hollard’s Risk Appetite and 
approving its RMS.  
HNZ related risk matters are incorporated within the Commercial function’s risk profile and are 
reviewed in the Commercial function’s quarterly risk forums. Material risks related to the NZ 
business that require prioritised focus are reported to the quarterly HNZ Management Committee 
(HNZMC) and Hollard Financial and Non-Financial Risk Management Committees (FRC and NFRC). 
Material risks that require further escalation are then reported by the Chief Risk Officer (CRO) to 
the BRC, or via the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) HNZ Report to the Board. See Figure 2. for further 
details.

Climate-related risk management processes, tools and methods 
Hollard’s approach to managing its material risks (including material climate-related risk) involves 
an assessment of the potential inherent and residual impact (both financial and non-financial) of 
each risk, the likelihood of that risk occurring, and the estimated time-horizon over which the impact 
of a risk may arise.  The outcome of this assessment is then compared against the risk appetite for 
each material risk.  Where a material risk is outside of appetite, it is raised through various 
governance committees such as the HNZMC, Financial and Non-Financial Risk Management 
Committee and Board Risk Committee, where discussions surrounding actions to bring the risks 
back within appetite take place. 
Climate risk is not assessed in its own right; instead, Hollard assesses the impact of climate on each 
of our established risk categories.  A number of tools and methods are used to assess the impact of 
climate-related risk on our risk categories, including but are not limited to:   
• Natural peril pricing review: Hollard assesses the appropriateness of its natural peril model on 
an annual basis to ensure that its exposure to perils is being appropriately priced, and to identify 
any new areas of risk; 
• Capital modelling and management: Hollard conducts quarterly stress testing to assess the 
impact of catastrophe risk (a type of acute physical climate risk) on capital, in line with the ICAAP. 
The stress scenarios considered include a single extreme event as well as multiple large events; 
• Catastrophe renewal modelling: uses detailed risk and exposure information to model Hollard’s 
catastrophe risk exposure annually to inform pricing, reinsurance purchasing, capital modelling 
and budgeting; 
• Embargo management: is conducted based on catastrophe events to limit risk concentration 
where there is a high probability of a natural peril event leading to unplanned claims cost; 
• Aggregate exposure and peril monitoring: Hollard (including HNZ) monitors aggregate exposure 
quarterly to prevent unplanned growth in high event risk areas; 
• Partner monitoring: Hollard administers partner oversight on a monthly or quarterly basis for 
risks, such as underwriting and pricing risks.

Appendix A: Definitions (supplemented by NZ CS 3 Appendix A) 
Climate-related risk: The potential for negative consequences from the impacts of climate change.  
Climate-related physical risk: Risk related to the physical impacts of a changing climate. These risks 
can be event-driven (acute) such as increased severity of extreme weather events. They can also be 
chronic, such as those related to longer-term shifts in precipitation and temperature and sea level 
rise. 
Climate-related transition risk: Risks related to the transition to a low-emission, climate-resilient 
global and domestic economy.  These risks are often categorised as policy, legal, technology, market 
and reputation risks associated with the mitigation and adaptation requirements relating to climate 
change. 
ESG: Environment, Social and Governance 
GHG: Greenhouse gas. The greenhouse gases listed in the Kyoto Protocol: carbon dioxide (CO2); 
methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), nitrogen trifluoride (NF3), 
perfluorocarbons (PFCs), and sulphur hexafluoride (SF6). 
Material: Information is material if omitting, misstating or obscuring it could reasonably be 
expected to influence decisions that primary users make on the basis of an entity’s climate-related 
disclosures. 
Scenario analysis: A process for systematically exploring the effects of a range of plausible future 
events under conditions of uncertainty. Engaging in this process helps an entity to identify its 
climate-related risks and opportunities and develop a better understanding of the resilience of its 
business model and strategy. 
Target: A specific level, threshold, or quantity of a metric that an entity wishes to meet over a 
defined time horizon.  They are often set in order to quantify an entity’s overall climate-related 
ambition and strategy. 
Transition plan: An aspect of an entity’s overall strategy that describes an entity’s targets, including 
any interim targets, and actions for its transition towards a low-emissions, climate-resilient future. 
Value chain: The full range of activities, resources and relationships related to an entity’s business 
model and the external environment in which it operates. A value chain encompasses the activities, 
resources and relationships an entity uses and relies on to create its products or services, from 
conception to delivery, consumption and end of life. Relevant activities, resources and relationships 
include those in an entity’s operations, such as human resources; those along its supply, marketing 
and distribution channels, such as materials and service sourcing and product and service sale and 
delivery; and the financing, geographical, geopolitical and regulatory environments in which an 
entity operates.

Director’s responsibilities for the GHG disclosures 
 
Directors are responsible for the preparation and fair presentation of the Selected GHG Disclosures in accordance with 
NZ CSs, which includes determining and disclosing the appropriate standard or standards used to measure its GHG 
emissions. This responsibility includes the design, implementation and maintenance of internal controls relevant to 
the preparation of GHG disclosures that are free from material misstatement whether due to fraud or error. 
 
Inherent uncertainty in preparing Selected GHG Disclosures 
 
Non-financial information, such as that included in the Climate-related Disclosure Statement, is subject to more 
inherent limitations than financial information, given both its nature and the methods used and assumptions applied 
in determining, calculating and sampling or estimating such information. GHG quantification is subject to inherent 
uncertainty because of incomplete scientific knowledge used to determine emissions factors and the values needed 
to combine emissions of different gases. 
 
As the procedures performed for this engagement are not performed continuously throughout the relevant period 
and the procedures performed in respect of the Branch’s compliance with NZ CSs are undertaken on a test basis, our 
limited assurance engagement cannot be relied on to detect all instances where the Branch may not have complied 
with the NZ CSs. Because of these inherent limitations, it is possible that fraud, error or non-compliance may occur 
and not be detected. 
 
In addition, we note that a limited assurance engagement is not designed to detect all instances of non-compliance 
with the NZ CSs, as it generally comprises making enquires, primarily of the responsible party, and applying analytical 
and other review procedures. 
 
Our responsibilities 
Our responsibility is to express an independent limited assurance conclusion on the Selected GHG Disclosures, based 
on the procedures we have performed and the evidence we have obtained. We conducted our limited assurance 
engagement in accordance with NZ SAE 1 and International Standard on Assurance Engagements (New Zealand) 3410: 
Assurance Engagements on Greenhouse Gas Statements (‘ISAE (NZ) 3410’), issued by the XRB. These standards require 
that we plan and perform this engagement to obtain limited assurance about whether the Selected GHG Disclosures 
are free from material misstatement.

Summary of work performed 
 
Our limited assurance engagement was performed in accordance with NZ SAE 1 and ISAE (NZ) 3410. This involves 
assessing the suitability in the circumstances of Branch’s use of NZ CSs as the basis for the preparation of the Selected 
GHG Disclosures, assessing the risks of material misstatement of the Selected GHG Disclosures whether due to fraud 
or error, responding to the assessed risks as necessary in the circumstances, and evaluating the overall presentation 
of the Selected GHG Disclosures. A limited assurance engagement is substantially less in scope than a reasonable 
assurance engagement in relation to both the risk assessment procedures, including an understanding of internal 
control, and the procedures performed in response to the assessed risks. 
 
The procedures we performed were based on our professional judgement and included enquiries, observation of 
processes performed, inspection of documents, analytical procedures, evaluating the appropriateness of 
quantification methods and reporting policies, and agreeing or reconciling with underlying records. In undertaking our 
limited assurance engagement on the Selected GHG Disclosures, we: 
 
• 
Obtained, through inquiries, an understanding of the Branch’s control environment, processes and information 
systems relevant to the preparation of the GHG disclosures. We did not evaluate the design of particular control 
activities, or obtain evidence about their implementation. 
• 
Evaluated whether the Branch’s methods for developing estimates are appropriate and had been consistently 
applied. Our procedures did not include testing the data on which the estimates are based or separately 
developing our own estimates against which to evaluate the Branch’s estimates. 
• 
Performed analytical procedures on particular emission categories by comparing the expected GHGs emitted to 
actual GHGs emitted and made enquiries of management to obtain explanations for any significant differences 
we identified. Where required we have undertaken substantive tests to examine supporting evidence. 
• Considered the presentation and disclosure of the GHG disclosures.

The procedures performed in a limited assurance engagement vary in nature and timing from, and are less in extent 
than for, a reasonable assurance engagement. Consequently, the level of assurance obtained in a limited assurance 
engagement is substantially lower than the assurance that would have been obtained had we performed a reasonable 
assurance engagement. Accordingly, we do not express a reasonable assurance opinion about whether Selected GHG 
Disclosures are fairly presented and prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with NZ CSs.
